title: Optimal Search Strategies under Finite Resource Constraints: The Role of Environmental Memory and Directional Information in Informed and Blind Protocols
abstract: Improving the efficiency of a stochastic search often requires to provide the searching agent with resources that modify its dynamics and help it explore space more quickly. Although such resources are often assumed to be unlimited and treated as a cost to mitigate, many realistic search processes operate under a finite resource budget, e.g. in processes with environmental memory in which the searcher deposits long-lasting cues along its path that it can interact with at later times to guide its further search. Here, we address the question of how to allocate a limited budget to maximize search efficiency by investigating a one-dimensional diffusing agent whose access to resources is constrained. We consider three resource models, namely an external force applied by an external controller to pull the searcher towards the target, directional flags deposited by the searcher along its path that redirect its motion towards the target, and self-generated chemorepulsive cues that act as a force field. For all these models, we find that resource usage should be concentrated in narrow regions of space when information about the searcher's current and past positions is available. In contrast, in blind strategies where a predefined time protocol is followed, resources should be used at a steady rate to ensure it to be used at most of its capacity by the time it reaches the target. We further show that blind strategies in non-Markovian processes with environmental memory are significantly less efficient due to the inherent fluctuations in the locations of deposited cues.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to optimize search efficiency for a diffusing particle when resources are limited. It rigorously compares 'informed' strategies, which use location-specific knowledge, against 'blind' strategies, which use time-based protocols. The findings show that utilizing environmental memory optimally requires spatially concentrated resource application, significantly outperforming blind resource expenditure.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to optimize the efficiency of a stochastic search process when the search agent operates under a finite budget of resources.
main_result: Optimal resource allocation requires concentrating resource usage in narrow spatial regions when information about the search history is available (informed strategy), whereas blind strategies require a steady rate of resource expenditure over time.
method: The authors analyze the Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) for various resource models (external force, directional flags, chemotactic cues) by solving the Fokker-Planck equation and applying variational principles.
model_or_system: The model involves a one-dimensional diffusing agent searching for a fixed target, constrained by a finite resource budget (work $W$ or heat $Q$). Resource application can be informed (state-dependent) or blind (time-dependent).
key_observables: Mean First Passage Time (MFPT), optimal force profiles, and the ratio of MFPTs between informed and blind protocols.
important_parameters: Finite work budget ($W$), diffusion constant ($D$), and system length ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares protocols based on whether the resource usage depends on the searcher's current/past position (informed) or follows a fixed time schedule (blind).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate optimal force profiles (piecewise linear) for external pulling strategies and compare MFPTs for informed versus blind protocols.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares optimal search strategies under finite resources, first analyzing external pulling forces (Section III), then directional flags (Section IV), and finally generalizing to auto-chemotactic cues, contrasting informed vs. blind protocols throughout.
why_interesting: The concepts of environmental memory and resource-constrained dynamics are highly relevant to open quantum systems, where environmental coupling acts as a dissipative resource, and optimal control strategies are crucial for quantum state preparation or measurement.
